title: Insurance Basics
summary: Map the risks → Decode the terms → Protect your income → Be ready to claim
subtitle: Translate the policy before asking it to protect the household

blocks.text: Insurance is a contract for sharing financial risk, written in a dialect that sometimes seems to charge by the syllable.

This lesson won’t choose a product, insurer or coverage amount for you. It will help you find the losses your household couldn’t absorb, decode the terms that decide what gets paid, compare quotes fairly and get ready for a claim or complaint. The policy sets the real terms, not the ad or a friendly summary.
Insurance doesn’t stop an emergency. It decides which covered losses get paid, up to what limit, after what deductible, and only within its exclusions and conditions.

items.title: “Insurance covers anything bad that happens.”
items.text: A policy covers set events, property, people and amounts, within its exclusions, deductibles, limits and conditions. Maintenance, wear and some hazards may be excluded or need an add-on.

blocks.text: Pay for the protection you need, and stop paying for the protection you don’t.
blocks.detail: Knowing which losses would sink your household, and how each policy responds, turns a pile of quotes into an honest choice.
blocks.extra: Section 02 maps the six kinds of coverage most households use.

sections.title: Map What You Can’t Afford to Lose

blocks.text: Start with your household, not with a product. Ask one question about each risk: if this happened tomorrow, could we pay for it from savings without lasting harm? If the answer is yes, you may not need to insure it. If it’s no, it belongs on your map.

items.title: HOME OR TENANT
items.text: Covers your belongings, your liability if someone is hurt or you damage someone else’s property, and extra living costs if you must move out after a covered loss. Overland flooding and sewer backup are often add-ons you have to ask for.

items.title: AUTO
items.text: Required by law in every province. In British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, basic coverage comes from a public insurer. In Quebec, a public plan covers injuries and private insurers cover the car itself.

items.title: LIFE
items.text: Pays money to the people who depend on your income or care if you die. Term insurance covers a set number of years and usually costs far less than permanent insurance.

items.title: DISABILITY
items.text: Replaces part of your income if illness or injury stops you working. For many working-age adults, being unable to work for months is far more likely than dying, yet it’s the cover people most often skip.

items.title: HEALTH AND DENTAL
items.text: Your provincial plan covers doctors and hospital care. Most prescriptions outside hospital, dental care, glasses and physiotherapy need a workplace plan, a private plan or a public program you qualify for.

items.title: TRAVEL
items.text: Your provincial plan pays little for care outside Canada, sometimes even in another province. A hospital stay in the United States can cost tens of thousands of dollars, so check coverage before every trip.

blocks.text: Check what you already have before you buy. Workplace benefits, a credit card’s travel or purchase coverage, and a partner’s plan may cover more than you think, or less. Get each one’s terms in writing.

sections.title: Six Terms That Control the Outcome

blocks.text: Decode the contract

items.title: Premium
items.text: The amount charged for coverage.

items.title: Deductible
items.text: The amount you pay toward a covered claim before the insurer pays the rest.

items.title: Coverage limit
items.text: The most the insurer will pay under that coverage.

items.title: Exclusion
items.text: A loss, cause, person, property or situation the policy does not cover.

items.title: Endorsement
items.text: A written change to the policy.

items.title: Settlement basis
items.text: Replacement cost and actual cash value can mean different payouts.

blocks.text: Compare quotes using the same property, limits, deductibles, add-ons and assumptions. A lower premium can mean a real saving, more of the risk landing on you, less coverage, or a mix of all three. Ask for the differences in writing.
The deductible trade-off
Two quotes for the same home
blocks.detail: Yearly premium and what you pay on a claim

items.title: Policy A
items.text: $1,560 a year — with a $500 deductible.

items.title: Policy B
items.text: $1,320 a year — with a $1,500 deductible.

items.title: The trade
items.text: B saves $240 a year — but costs $1,000 more each time you claim.

items.title: Break-even
items.text: About 4 years — if you claim less often than once every four years, B usually comes out ahead.

blocks.text: A higher deductible only works if the money is ready when you need it. Save your deductible in your emergency fund, and use the calculator to see how long it takes.

items.title: “The cheapest premium is the cheapest policy overall.”
items.text: Price is only one layer. Compare limits, deductibles, exclusions, add-ons, how claims are paid, service and how much of a loss lands back on your household.

blocks.text: FCAC: How insurance works

sections.title: Nina and the Quote That Won by $18

blocks.text: Nina and the quote that won by $18
paragraphs: Nina Patel moves from a rented Ottawa apartment into a small townhouse. Her old tenant policy was easy to ignore, which is a sentence insurance policies hear just before they become important. She gets two home-policy quotes. One is $18 cheaper each month. The decision looks finished.

Then Nina’s brother asks if both quotes cover the same things. They don’t. The cheaper quote has a higher deductible, a lower limit for valuables and no sewer-backup endorsement. One quote pays replacement cost for listed items. The other is unclear. Nina isn’t sure which differences matter. The price is doing an excellent job of distracting everyone.

Nina makes a room-by-room inventory with photos, model numbers and receipts. She lists the risks she could not cover alone: liability, a big loss of belongings and a place to stay if she has to leave home. Then she sends each licensed agent the same written questions. They cover limits, deductibles, exclusions, water damage, payout basis, endorsements and claims service. ‘Show me how each contract responds to these risks.’

The answers show that the cheaper price partly comes from leaving more risk with Nina. She picks the contract whose written terms fit her needs, puts the deductible in her emergency fund and stores the policy, inventory and claims number away from the home.

Months later, a supply line bursts and ruins her flooring and some belongings. Nina shuts off the water safely, protects the area, takes photos and calls the insurer. She keeps her receipts and holds on to the damaged items until she is told what to do. The claim takes patience and proof. But she does not have to rebuild her household from memory. She compared the risk, not the loudest price.

blocks.text: A home inventory helps you choose coverage and prove a claim. Keep the photos, receipts, serial numbers and policy somewhere you can reach even if your home or phone can’t be.
A burst pipe found Nina ready, because she built her evidence file months before she needed it.
blocks.detail: Proof gathered in a calm month turns a claim into a checklist instead of a scramble from memory.
blocks.extra: Section 05 looks at the risk most households forget: losing their income.

sections.title: Protect Your Income, Not Just Your Things

blocks.text: Your ability to earn is usually your household’s biggest asset. A house fire is rare. A few months off work after surgery, an injury or a mental-health crisis is much more common.
Where income protection comes from

items.title: EI sickness benefits
items.text: Up to 26 weeks — at 55% of your insurable earnings, to a maximum of about $729 a week in 2026, if you have enough insured hours.

items.title: Workplace disability plan
items.text: Often 60% to 70% — of your pay, for short-term and then long-term disability. Ask HR for the booklet.

items.title: CPP disability
items.text: For severe and prolonged disability — a monthly benefit if you can’t work at any job on a regular basis.

items.title: Private disability insurance
items.text: For gaps — useful if you’re self-employed or have no workplace plan.

blocks.text: To estimate life insurance needs, add up the debts you’d want paid off, the income your family would need for a set number of years and final costs. Then subtract your savings and the coverage you already have. A licensed advisor can check your numbers, but you’ll understand the answer better if you do the rough math first.

Be careful with insurance sold with a loan or credit card, called creditor insurance. It can cost more for the coverage you get, the payout usually goes to the lender, and some claims are reviewed only after you claim. You have the right to cancel it, and you can’t be forced to buy it to get the loan.

items.title: “My workplace plan has me covered.”
items.text: It may, but group coverage usually ends when the job does, and the amount may be a set multiple of your salary that won’t cover everything. Read the booklet and note what happens if you leave.

blocks.text: Most of a claim’s success is decided in the first few days. Follow these steps in order.

items.title: Protect people first
items.text: Call emergency services when needed, and prevent further damage only when it is safe to do so.

items.title: Notify promptly
items.text: Check the policy’s steps and deadline, then contact the insurer or your representative as soon as you can.

items.title: Document carefully
items.text: Photograph the damage, list the items, keep receipts and write down your conversations. Ask before repairing or throwing anything out, except for urgent safety steps.

items.title: Escalate in order
items.text: Use the insurer’s own complaint process and ask for its final decision. If the problem is still not resolved, you may take it to the right ombudservice or provincial regulator.

blocks.text: Water damage isn’t one single coverage. Flooding, sewer backup, overland water, a burst pipe and normal wear can each be treated differently. Read the definitions and exclusions, and ask whether an add-on is available.
If you disagree with a decision

Ask for the decision and the reason in writing, and send any missing proof. Use the insurer’s own complaint process first. If you still disagree, a free ombudservice can review it: the General Insurance OmbudService for home and auto, or the OmbudService for Life and Health Insurance for life, disability and health. Your provincial insurance regulator can confirm an agent’s licence and explain your options.

If an insurer fails, policyholders have protection. Assuris protects life and health policies, and the Property and Casualty Insurance Compensation Corporation (PACICC) protects home and auto policies, up to set limits.

items.title: “If a claim is denied, there’s nothing I can do.”
items.text: Ask for the decision in writing, add missing evidence, use the complaint process and, if needed, go to the ombudservice, the regulator or a lawyer.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: How is a premium different from coverage?
items.detail: The premium is the price you pay. Coverage is the protection the policy’s terms, limits and conditions give you.

items.title: What trade-off can accompany a higher deductible?
items.detail: A lower premium may shift more of the upfront claim cost onto the household.

items.title: How does an exclusion differ from an endorsement?
items.detail: An exclusion removes coverage for something specific. An endorsement is a written change to the policy.

items.title: Why compare two quotes on like-for-like terms?
items.detail: Different terms can mean the two prices are buying different protection.

items.title: What should happen first after a loss, and what evidence should be preserved?
items.detail: Protect people first. Prevent more damage only when it is safe. Tell the insurer promptly and keep photos, lists, receipts, damaged items and notes on every call.

items.title: Policy B saves $240 a year but has a $1,000 higher deductible. Roughly how often can you claim before it costs more?
items.detail: Less than about once every four years: $1,000 ÷ $240 ≈ 4.

items.title: Which free service reviews unresolved home and auto insurance complaints?

blocks.text: Agents and brokers must be licensed where they work. Regulators can confirm a licence and explain complaint routes, but they won’t rewrite a policy after a loss.

Use this page to prepare questions, not to make a personal coverage decision. Record where policies are kept and general contacts, but leave out passwords, full ID numbers or sensitive medical details.

Review coverage after a move, a renovation or a big purchase. Review it again after a new driver, business use, a relationship change or an income change. A policy can stay active while going out of date with remarkable professionalism.
Compare the risk transfer, not the loudest price.
blocks.detail: Read the policy terms. Compare quotes on equal coverage. Save the deductible. Get your evidence and claim steps ready before the household needs them.

items.title: Premium
items.text: The amount charged for insurance coverage.

items.title: Deductible
items.text: The amount you pay toward an eligible claim before the insurer pays the rest.

items.title: Coverage limit
items.text: The most the insurer will pay under a particular coverage.

items.title: Exclusion
items.text: A loss, cause, person, property or situation the policy does not cover.

items.title: Endorsement
items.text: A written change to the policy.

items.title: Actual cash value
items.text: A payout that generally reflects an item’s value after wear and age, based on the policy wording.

items.title: Replacement cost
items.text: A payout basis that pays to replace covered property, within the policy’s rules and limits.

items.title: Creditor insurance
items.text: Insurance sold with a loan or credit card that pays the lender if you die, become disabled or lose your job.

items.title: Ombudservice
items.text: A free, independent service that reviews complaints you couldn’t resolve with the company.
